Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians

The Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians is a distinct government whose public history connects Anishinaabeg fishing communities around the upper Great Lakes with later organizing at Sugar Island. Its account describes summer gatherings at Bahweting and family seasonal work, then follows colonial pressures and the building of a separate tribal government. The recognition narrative explains why Sugar Island organizers sought a government distinct from Bay Mills; that attributed history should not be flattened into interchangeable regional names. It records recognition in 1972 and subsequent constitutional organization. The Tribe's Language and Culture Division provides a second entry point, linking Anishinaabemowin with education, repatriation and historic preservation, a culture camp and a learning center. This selection introduces a particular community's history and living institutions without claiming to cover all Ojibwe peoples. Population totals, current service access, exact treaty consequences and measured language outcomes remain outside this guide. The dated sources invite further reading and comparison rather than supplying community endorsement or exhaustive history.

01

Organizing a particular government

The historical narrative traces meetings among Sugar Island residents into a campaign for separate recognition. It records 1972 recognition and a constitution adopted afterward. Read this as the Tribe's account of organizing and continuity; precise treaty and legal conclusions require the underlying documents.

Read the sources [1] Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians

02

Language and cultural responsibilities

The Division identifies language, repatriation and historic preservation, a culture camp, and a learning center as parts of its work. Its public description connects cultural continuity with institutions. It does not establish present schedules, access to every activity or measured learning outcomes.
